title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 883–884 (Night 210, continuing nights-209), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 210 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. On the third night the disguised Lady Budūr comes to the bridal chamber, weeps for her lost husband and recites verses, and is about to rise to pray when Ḥayāt al-Nufūs catches her by the skirt and reproaches her: her father King Armānūs has resolved that, unless the marriage is consummated this night, he will strip his son-in-law of the kingdom, banish him, and perhaps kill him. Torn between ruin and exposure, Budūr reasons that the Ebony Islands are the only road by which Qamar al-Zamān can come home, so she must keep her throne; she tells the princess her whole story, shows her that she is a woman, and begs her to keep the secret until God reunites her with her beloved; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْعَاشِرَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ʿāshiratu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the tenth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and tenth night,
sentences.n: “The tenth after the two hundred”: al-ʿāshira, “the tenth”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَلِكَ أَرْمَانُوسَ لَمَّا اتَّفَقَ مَعَ ابْنَتِهِ عَلَى هٰذَا الْكَلَامِ وَأَضْمَرَ عَلَى هٰذَا الرَّأْيِ وَأَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ قَامَتِ الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ مِنْ دَسْتِ الْمَمْلَكَةِ إِلَى الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika Armānūsa lammā ittafaqa maʿa ibnatihi ʿalā hādhā al-kalāmi wa-aḍmara ʿalā hādhā al-raʾyi wa-aqbala al-laylu qāmati al-malikatu Budūru min dasti al-mamlakati ilā al-qaṣri
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that King Armānūs, when he-agreed with his-daughter upon this the-speech and-resolved-secretly upon this the-view, and-came-on the-night, rose the-Queen Budūr from (the) seat (of) the-kingdom to the-palace.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when King Armānūs had agreed on this with his daughter and inwardly settled on that course, and night came on, Queen Budūr rose from the seat of the kingdom and went to the palace.
sentences.n: The print runs al-saʿīdu anna, “fortunate, that”, together as one word, السعيدان, as at the start of the last night; it is kept as set. The night takes up the last sentence of the one before. The sentence that anna, “that”, opens is never finished: it begins with King Armānūs, and after the lammā-clause, “when he had agreed”, the narrator turns to Budūr and makes her the subject of qāmat, “she rose”, a loose join common in the storyteller's Arabic. Armānūsa is accusative after anna, with the diptote's -a. ittafaqa maʿa … ʿalā, Form VIII, “to agree with someone on something”; aḍmara ʿalā, Form IV, “to resolve on in secret”, with the later ʿalā. dast, a Persian word, “seat of honour, throne”: dast al-mamlaka, “the seat of the kingdom”, the place where she sits to govern by day. The hamza of الرأي is printed.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلَتِ الْمَكَانَ الَّذِي هُوَ مُعَدٌّلَهَا فَرَأَتِ الشَّمْعَ مَوْقُودًا وَالسَّيِّدَةَ حَيَاةَ النُّفُوسِ جَالِسَةً
sentences.tr: wa-dakhalati al-makāna alladhī huwa muʿaddun lahā fa-raʾati al-shamʿa mawqūdan wa-al-sayyidata Ḥayāta al-Nufūsi jālisatan
sentences.l: And-she-entered the-place which it (was) made-ready for-her, and-she-saw the-candles lit and-the-Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs sitting.
sentences.i: She went into the chamber that had been made ready for her, and saw the candles lit and the Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs sitting there.
sentences.n: The print runs muʿaddun lahā, “made ready for her”, together as one word, معدّلها; it is kept as set, and the tanwīn of muʿaddun is written on the dāl inside it. muʿadd, passive participle of Form IV aʿadda, “to make ready”; li- marks the one it is meant for. Its shadda is printed. mawqūdan and jālisatan are accusatives of state (ḥāl): “lit”, “sitting”. al-sayyidata Ḥayāta al-Nufūsi is the second object of raʾat, “she saw”. The hamza of فرأت is printed.

sentences.t: فَتَذَكَّرَتْ زَوْجَهَا وَمَا جَرَى لَهُمَا مِنَ الْفُرْقَةِ بَيْنَهُمَا فِي تِلْكَ الْمُدَّةِ الْيَسِيرَةِ فَبَكَتْ وَتَنَهَّدَتْ وَوَالَتِ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-tadhakkarat zawjahā wa-mā jarā lahumā mina al-furqati baynahumā fī tilka al-muddati al-yasīrati fa-bakat wa-tanahhadat wa-wālati al-zafarāti wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And-she-remembered her-husband and-what befell (the) two-of-them of the-parting between-the-two-of-them in that the-span the-short; and-she-wept and-sighed and-made-follow-one-on-another the-groans, and-recited, saying, these the-verses:
sentences.i: She remembered her husband, and the parting that had come between the two of them after so short a time together, and she wept and sighed, and groan followed groan, and she recited these verses:
sentences.n: jarā li-, “to befall”: li- marks the ones it befalls. min al-furqati, “of separation”: min explains what it was that befell them. al-mudda al-yasīra, “the short span”, the few days of their marriage before they were parted. wālā, Form III, “to make one thing follow another”: wālat al-zafarāt, “she sent up sigh after sigh”. tanahhada, Form V, “to sigh”; its shadda is printed. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”: the imperfect describes the reciting.

sentences.t:
قَسَمًا لَقَدْ مَلَاَتْ اَحَادِيثِي الْفَضَا * كَالشَّمْسِ مُشْرِقَةً عَلَى ذَاتِ الْغَضَا
نَطَقَتْ اِشَارَتُهُ فَاَشْكَلَ فَهْمُهَا * فَلِذَاكَ شَوْقِي فِي الْمَزِيدِ وَمَا انْقَضَى
اَبْغَضْتُ حُسْنَ الصَّبْرِ مُذْ اَحْبَبْتُهُ * اَرَأَيْتَ صَبًّا فِى الصَّبَابَةِ مُبْغِضَا
وَمُمَرِّضِ اللَّحْظَاتِ صَالَ بِفَتْكِهَا * وَاللَّحْظُ اَقْتَلُ مَا يَكُونُ مُمَرِّضَا
اَلْقَى ذَوَائِبَهُ وَحَطَّ لِثَامَهُ * فَرَايْتُ مِنْهُ الْحُسْنَ اَسْوَدَ اَبْيَضَا
سُقْمِي وَبُرْئِي فِي يَدَيْهِ وَاِنَّمَا * يَشْفِي سَقَامَ الْحُبِّ مَنْ قَدْ اَمْرَضَا
هَامَ الْوُشَاحُ بِرِقَّةٍ فِي خَصْرِهِ * وَالرِّدْفُ مِنْ حَسَدٍ اَبَى اَنْ يَنْهَضَا
وَكَاَنَّ طُرَّتَهُ وَضَوْءَ جَبِينِهِ * لَيْلُ دُجٰى فَاعْتَاقَهُ صُبْحٌ اَضَا
sentences.tr:
qasaman la-qad malaʾat aḥādīthī al-faḍā * ka-al-shamsi mushriqatan ʿalā dhāti al-ghaḍā
naṭaqat ishāratuhu fa-ashkala fahmuhā * fa-li-dhāka shawqī fī al-mazīdi wa-mā inqaḍā
abghaḍtu ḥusna al-ṣabri mudh aḥbabtuhu * a-raʾayta ṣabban fī al-ṣabābati mubghiḍā
wa-mumarriḍi al-laḥaẓāti ṣāla bi-fatkihā * wa-al-laḥẓu aqtalu mā yakūnu mumarriḍā
alqā dhawāʾibahu wa-ḥaṭṭa lithāmahu * fa-raʾaytu minhu al-ḥusna aswada abyaḍā
suqmī wa-burʾī fī yadayhi wa-innamā * yashfī saqāma al-ḥubbi man qad amraḍā
hāma al-wushāḥu bi-riqqatin fī khaṣrihi * wa-al-ridfu min ḥasadin abā an yanhaḍā
wa-kaʾanna ṭurratahu wa-ḍawʾa jabīnihi * laylu dujā fa-iʿtāqahu ṣubḥun aḍā
sentences.l:
By-an-oath! Indeed have-filled my-tales the-open-space, * like-the-sun rising upon Dhāt al-Ghaḍā.
Spoke his-sign, and-was-obscure (the) understanding-of-it; * so-for-that my-longing (is) in the-increase and-not ended.
I-hated (the) beauty (of) the-patience since I-loved-him: * have-you-seen a-lover in the-passion hating?
And-(many-a)-one-making-sick (his) glances, (who) assailed with-their-deadliness! * And-the-glance (is) most-killing (of) what it-is, sick.
He-let-fall his-locks and-put-down his-face-veil, * and-I-saw from-him the-beauty black, white.
My-sickness and-my-cure (are) in his-two-hands; and-only * heals (the) sickness (of) the-love (he) who has made-sick.
Wandered the-sash, through-slenderness, in his-waist, * and-the-buttocks, from envy, refused to rise.
And-as-if his-forelock and-(the)-light (of) his-brow * (were the) night (of) darkness, and-held-it-back a-morning (that) shone.
sentences.i:
I swear it: the tales of me have filled the open plain, * like the sun rising over Dhāt al-Ghaḍā.
His signs spoke, but what they meant was hard to grasp; * and so my longing ever grows and has not ended.
I have hated fair patience since I fell in love with him: * have you ever seen a lover who hates in his love?
Many a one whose glances languish has struck with their deadliness, * and a glance is deadliest when it is languid.
He let down his locks and drew aside his veil, * and I saw in him beauty both black and white.
My sickness and my cure are both in his hands, * and only he who brought on the sickness of love can heal it.
The sash strays loose, so slender is his waist, * and his buttocks, out of envy, refuse to rise.
It is as though his forelock and the brightness of his brow * were a night of darkness, held back by a morning that shone.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is kāmil, and every line rhymes in -ḍā. Budūr, alone with the bride, speaks of her lost husband as “he”. qasaman, “by an oath!”, an accusative standing for “I swear an oath”, answered by la-qad. malaʾat, “have filled”, printed مَلَاَتْ, the hamza unwritten. al-faḍā and aḍā are faḍāʾ, “open space”, and aḍāʾa, “it shone”, with the final hamza dropped for the rhyme. Dhāt al-Ghaḍā, “the place of the ghaḍā”, a desert shrub whose wood burns long and hot, is a place name of the old poetry. ashkala, Form IV, “to be obscure, hard to make out”. fī al-mazīd, “on the increase”. ḥusn al-ṣabr, “fair patience”, the patience that love-poets refuse; ṣabb, “one burning with love”, and ṣabāba, “ardent love”, play on ṣabr. In the third line the question means: a lover hates nothing, yet I hate patience. In the fourth line wa- stands for rubba, “many a”: wa-mumarriḍi al-laḥaẓāti, “many a one who makes his glances languish”; ṣāla bi-, “to assail with”: bi- marks the weapon. aqtalu mā yakūnu mumarriḍā, “most deadly is it when it is languishing”. dhawāʾib, “locks, side-plaits”, plural of dhuʾāba; lithām, the veil drawn over the lower face. The print writes raʾaytu as رَايْتُ, with no hamza and the alif standing bare; the metre wants raʾaytu, and that is how it is read. “Black and white”: his hair black, his face white. amraḍa, Form IV, “to make sick”. wushāḥ (more often wishāḥ), a broad jewelled sash worn slanting from shoulder to hip; hāma, “to wander, stray as one distracted by love”, of a sash that hangs loose on a slender waist. ridf, “buttocks, hindquarters”, heavy and slow to rise, a beauty in the poets' eyes; they envy the waist, or the waist them. ṭurra, “forelock, the fringe of hair over the brow”. iʿtāqa, Form VIII, “to hold back, hinder”: the dark hair is a night that the bright brow, a morning, holds back. dujā, “darkness”, is printed with a dagger alif (دُجٰى). The hamza in the middle of اَرَأَيْتَ and that of ذَوَائِبَهُ, وَبُرْئِي and وَضَوْءَ is printed; the print sets a bare alif without hamza in مَلَاَتْ, اَحَادِيثِي, اِشَارَتُهُ, فَاَشْكَلَ, اَبْغَضْتُ, اَحْبَبْتُهُ, the first alif of اَرَأَيْتَ, اَقْتَلُ, اَلْقَى, فَرَايْتُ, اَسْوَدَ, اَبْيَضَا, وَاِنَّمَا, اَمْرَضَا, اَبَى, اَنْ, وَكَاَنَّ and اَضَا, and writes fī as فِى once; all are kept.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ إِنْشَادِهَا أَرَادَتْ أَنْ تَقُومَ إِلَى الصَّلٰوةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min inshādihā arādat an taqūma ilā al-ṣalāti
sentences.l: And-when she-finished from her-reciting, she-wanted to rise to the-prayer.
sentences.i: When she had finished her recital she was about to rise to pray,
sentences.n: faragha min, “to be done with”: min marks what is finished. al-ṣalāh, “prayer”, is printed الصلٰوة, in the old spelling with wāw and the dagger alif, as in the Qurʾān; the dagger alif is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِحَيَاةِ النُّفُوسِ مَسَكَتْهَا مِنْ ذَيْلِهَا وَتَعَلَّقَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi masakat-hā min dhaylihā wa-taʿallaqat
sentences.l: And-behold, Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, she-caught-her by her-skirt and-clung.
sentences.i: when all at once Ḥayāt al-Nufūs caught her by the hem of her robe and clung to her.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. masaka, “to take hold of”, the later form of Classical amsaka; min marks the part held, “by her skirt”. taʿallaqa, Form V, “to cling”, here without its usual bi-, “to”.

sentences.t: وَقٰلَتْ لَهَا يَاسَيِّدِي أَمَا تَسْتَحِي مِنْ وَالِدِي وَمَا فَعَلَ مَعَكَ مِنَ الْجَمِيلِ وَأَنْتَ تَتْرُكُنِي إِلَى هٰذَا الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahā yā sayyidī a-mā tastaḥī min wālidī wa-mā faʿala maʿaka mina al-jamīli wa-anta tatrukunī ilā hādhā al-waqti
sentences.l: And-she-said to-her: O my-lord, do-not you-feel-shame before my-father and-what he-did with-you of the-kindness, while-you leave-me until this the-time?
sentences.i: She said to her, “My lord, have you no shame before my father, after all the kindness he has shown you, that you leave me untouched to this day?”
sentences.n: قلت is printed for قَالَتْ, “she said”, a defective spelling; the dagger alif shows the long vowel. yā sayyidī, “O my lord”, is set as one word (ياسيدي); it is kept as set. Ḥayāt al-Nufūs speaks to Budūr as to a man, “my lord”, and with the masculine -ka and anta. a-mā, “do … not?”, a question that reproaches. tastaḥī, “you feel shame”, Form X of ḥayiya, the later form of Classical tastaḥyī; istaḥā min, “to be ashamed before”: min marks the one before whom. wa-mā faʿala maʿaka mina al-jamīli, “and (before) what he has done for you of kindness”: mā is joined to wālidī under the same min; faʿala maʿa, “to do for” someone; min explains mā. wa-anta tatrukunī, “while you leave me”: a clause of state. taraka, “to leave, let alone”: here, to leave the bride untouched.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مِنْهَا ذٰلِكَ جَلَسَتْ عَلَى حَيْلِهَا فِي مَكَانِهَا وَقَالَتْ يَاحَبِيبَتِي مَا الَّذِي تَقُولِينَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat minhā dhālika jalasat ʿalā ḥaylihā fī makānihā wa-qālat yā ḥabībatī mā alladhī taqūlīnahu
sentences.l: And-when she-heard from-her that, she-sat on her-strength in her-place and-said: O my-beloved, what (is) that-which you-are-saying-it?
sentences.i: When she heard this from her, she sat bolt upright where she was and said, “My dear, what is this you are saying?”
sentences.n: jalasa ʿalā ḥaylihi, “to sit up on one's strength”, that is, to sit up straight: ḥayl, “strength”, is an old by-form of ḥawl, but the phrase belongs to the spoken language. yā ḥabībatī, “O my beloved”, is set as one word (ياحبيبتي); it is kept as set. mā alladhī taqūlīnahu, “what is it that you are saying?”: the -hu of taqūlīnahu returns to alladhī.

sentences.t: قَالَتِ الَّذِي أَقُولُهُ إِنِّي مَا رَأَيْتُ أَحَدًا مُعْجَبًا بِنَفْسِهِ مِثْلَكَ
sentences.tr: qālati alladhī aqūluhu innī mā raʾaytu aḥadan muʿjaban bi-nafsihi mithlaka
sentences.l: She-said: That-which I-say-it: I not I-have-seen anyone pleased with-himself like-you.
sentences.i: She said, “What I am saying is this: I have never seen anyone as taken with himself as you are.
sentences.n: alladhī aqūluhu innī …, “what I say is: I have not …”: what she says follows as it would after qāla, with inna, and stands as the predicate. muʿjab bi-nafsihi, “taken with himself, conceited”, passive participle of Form IV aʿjaba: bi- marks what one is taken with. mithlaka, “like you”, accusative as an adverb. The hamza of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: فَهَلْ كُلُّ مَنْ كَانَ مَلِيحًا يُعْجَبُ بِنَفْسِهِ هٰكَذَا
sentences.tr: fa-hal kullu man kāna malīḥan yuʿjabu bi-nafsihi hākadhā
sentences.l: So-is every who was handsome taken with-himself like-this?
sentences.i: Is everyone who is handsome so taken with himself?
sentences.n: yuʿjabu bi-nafsihi, passive of Form IV aʿjaba, “he is pleased with himself”: bi- marks what pleases him. malīḥ, “handsome, comely”, the later language's word for good looks.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ أَنَا مَا قُلْتُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تَرْغَبَ فِيَّ وَإِنَّمَا قُلْتُهُ خِيفَةً عَلَيْكَ مِنَ الْمَلِكِ أَرْمَانُوسَ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin anā mā qultu hādhā al-kalāma li-ajli an targhaba fiyya wa-innamā qultuhu khīfatan ʿalayka mina al-maliki Armānūsa
sentences.l: But I, not I-said this the-speech for-the-sake that you-desire in-me; and-only I-said-it (from) fear for-you from King Armānūs.
sentences.i: But I did not say this so that you would desire me; I said it only out of fear for you from King Armānūs,
sentences.n: li-ajli an, “for the sake of, so that”: li- gives the purpose. raghiba fī, “to desire”: the verb takes fī of the thing desired. The shadda of فيّ is printed. khīfatan, “out of fear”, an accusative giving the reason; khāfa ʿalā, “to fear for”, min, “of”. Armānūsa is genitive with the diptote's -a.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ أَضْمَرَ إِنْ لَمْ تَدْخُلْ عَلَيَّ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَتُزِيلْ بَكَارَتِي فَإِنَّهُ يُصْبِحُ يَنْزِعُكَ مِنَ الْمَمْلَكَةِ وَيُسَفِّرُكَ مِنْ بِلَادِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu aḍmara in lam tadkhul ʿalayya fī hādhihi al-laylati wa-tuzīl bakāratī fa-innahu yuṣbiḥu yanziʿuka mina al-mamlakati wa-yusaffiruka min bilādihi
sentences.l: For-indeed-he resolved-secretly: if not you-go-in upon-me in this the-night and-remove my-virginity, then-indeed-he (will) rise-in-the-morning stripping-you from the-kingdom and-sending-you-off from his-lands.
sentences.i: for he has made up his mind that if you do not go in to me tonight and take my maidenhead, in the morning he will strip you of the kingdom and send you out of his country.
sentences.n: aḍmara, Form IV, “to resolve in secret”: what he resolved follows directly, as a whole conditional sentence. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to” a bride, to consummate the marriage. The shadda of عليّ is printed. tuzīl, from azāla, Form IV, “to remove”: after lam the Classical jussive would be tuzil, but the print keeps the long ī (وتزيل), as the later language does, and as with yuzīl in the last night; it is kept. bakāra, “virginity”. fa-innahu …, “then he …”: the answer of the condition is a full sentence and so takes fa-. yuṣbiḥu yanziʿuka, “he will be, come morning, stripping you”: aṣbaḥa, “to be in the morning”, with an imperfect after it, “in the morning he will …”. nazaʿa min, “to pull out of, strip of”. saffara, Form II, “to send away on a journey”, here “to banish”.

sentences.t: وَرُبَّمَا يَزْدَادُ بِهِ الْغَيْظُ فَيَقْتُلُكَ
sentences.tr: wa-rubbamā yazdādu bihi al-ghayẓu fa-yaqtuluka
sentences.l: And-perhaps increases in-him the-rage, and-he-kills-you.
sentences.i: And perhaps his anger will grow so great that he will kill you.
sentences.n: rubbamā, “perhaps, it may be that”. izdāda, Form VIII of zāda, “to increase”; bihi, “in him”: bi- marks the one in whom it grows. ghayẓ, “rage, wrath”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا يَا سَيِّدِي رَحِمْتُكَ وَنَصَحْتُكَ وَالرَّأْيُ رَأْيُكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anā yā sayyidī raḥimtuka wa-naṣaḥtuka wa-al-raʾyu raʾyuka
sentences.l: And-I, O my-lord, I-pitied-you and-advised-you; and-the-view (is) your-view.
sentences.i: I, my lord, have taken pity on you and given you good counsel; the decision is yours.”
sentences.n: naṣaḥa, “to give sincere advice to”, takes the person directly. al-raʾyu raʾyuka, “the decision is yours”, a set phrase. The hamza of والرأي and رأيك is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ مِنْهَا ذٰلِكَ الْكَلَامَ أَطْرَقَتْ بِرَأْسِهَا إِلَى الْأَرْضِ وَحَارَتْ فِي أَمْرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿati al-malikatu Budūru minhā dhālika al-kalāma aṭraqat bi-raʾsihā ilā al-arḍi wa-ḥārat fī amrihā
sentences.l: And-when heard the-Queen Budūr from-her that the-speech, she-bowed with-her-head to the-ground and-was-perplexed in her-affair.
sentences.i: When Queen Budūr heard these words from her, she bowed her head to the ground and was at a loss what to do.
sentences.n: aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi, Form IV, “to bow one's head, look down in silence”: the verb takes bi- of the head it lowers. ḥāra fī amrihi, “to be at a loss in one's affair”. The print writes raʾs, “head”, as راس, without the hamza, as it usually does.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا إِنْ خَالَفْتُهُ هَلَكْتُ وَإِنْ أَطَعْتُهُ افْتَضَحْتُ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat fī nafsihā in khālaftuhu halaktu wa-in aṭaʿtuhu iftaḍaḥtu
sentences.l: Then she-said in herself: If I-oppose-him, I-perish; and-if I-obey-him, I-am-disgraced.
sentences.i: Then she said to herself, “If I defy him I am lost, and if I obey him I am disgraced.
sentences.n: qālat fī nafsihā, “she said in herself”, to herself. The two conditions run in parallel, perfect in both halves, halaktu answering iftaḍaḥtu. khālafa, Form III, “to go against, disobey”. iftaḍaḥa, Form VIII of faḍaḥa, “to be exposed, put to shame”: to obey would be to go in to the bride and be found a woman.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ أَنَا فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ مَلِكَةٌ عَلَى جَزَائِرِ الْآبَنُوسِ كُلِّهَا وَهِيَ تَحْتَ حُكْمِي
sentences.tr: wa-lākin anā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati malikatun ʿalā jazāʾiri al-ābanūsi kullihā wa-hiya taḥta ḥukmī
sentences.l: But I, in this the-hour, (am) a-queen over (the) Islands (of) the-Ebony, all-of-them, and-they (are) under my-rule.
sentences.i: But for now I am queen over all the Ebony Islands, and they are under my rule.
sentences.n: malikatun ʿalā, “queen over”. jazāʾir al-ābanūs, “the Islands of Ebony”: the realm of the City of Ebony, here called by its islands. kullihā, “all of them”, genitive to agree with jazāʾir. hiya, “they”, the feminine singular for a non-human plural. The ئ of جزائر and the آ of الآبنوس are printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَجْتَمِعُ أَنَا وَقَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ إِلَّا فِي هٰذَا الْمَوْضِعِ لِأَنَّهُ لَيْسَ لَهُ طَرِيقٌ إِلَى بِلَادِهِ إِلَّا مِنْ جَزَائِرِ الْآبَنُوسِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā ajtamiʿu anā wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni illā fī hādhā al-mawḍiʿi li-annahu laysa lahu ṭarīqun ilā bilādihi illā min jazāʾiri al-ābanūsi
sentences.l: And-not I-meet, I and-Qamar al-Zamān, except in this the-place, because-he, not-is to-him a-road to his-lands except from (the) Islands (of) the-Ebony.
sentences.i: And Qamar al-Zamān and I will meet again nowhere but here, for there is no road to his country except by way of the Ebony Islands.
sentences.n: mā ajtamiʿu … illā, “I will not meet … except”: the imperfect looks ahead. The print's اجتمع could also be read as the perfect, ijtamaʿa, “he met”, but the sense wants “I”: anā, “I”, is set after the verb so that wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni can be joined to it, “I and Qamar al-Zamān”. li-annahu, “because”: li- gives the reason. laysa lahu ṭarīqun, “he has no road”: li- marks the one who has it. The ئ of جزائر and the آ of الآبنوس are printed.

sentences.t: وَإِنِّي حِرْتُ فِي أَمْرِي وَفَوَّضْتُ أَمْرِي إِلَى اللّٰهِ فَهُوَ نِعْمَ الْمُدَبِّرُ
sentences.tr: wa-innī ḥirtu fī amrī wa-fawwaḍtu amrī ilā Allāhi fa-huwa niʿma al-mudabbiru
sentences.l: And-indeed-I, I-am-perplexed in my-affair, and-I-commit my-affair to God, for-He (is) how-excellent the-disposer!
sentences.i: I am at a loss what to do, and I commit my case to God, for He is the best of those who order things.
sentences.n: ḥirtu, “I am at a loss”, perfect 1cs of ḥāra. fawwaḍa amrahu ilā Allāh, Form II, “to commit one's affair to God”, a pious formula. niʿma, “how excellent is …!”, the verb of praise; al-mudabbir, “the one who orders and disposes things”, from Form II dabbara. Its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَنَا ذَكَرٌ حَتَّى أَقُومَ أَفْتَحُ هٰذِهِ الْبِنْتَ الْبِكْرَ
sentences.tr: wa-mā anā dhakarun ḥattā aqūma aftaḥu hādhihi al-binta al-bikra
sentences.l: And-not I (am) a-male, so-that I-should-rise (and) open this the-girl the-virgin.
sentences.i: I am no man, that I should set about opening this virgin girl.”
sentences.n: mā anā dhakarun, “I am not a male”: mā negates a nominal sentence, and its predicate stands in the nominative, as the later language has it. ḥattā aqūma, “so that I should rise”, subjunctive after ḥattā; qāma, “to rise”, before another verb means “to set about”. aftaḥu, “I open”, the imperfect set straight after it with no conjunction, the later language's way of chaining verbs. fataḥa, “to open”, of a virgin, to deflower. bikr, “virgin”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَةَ بُدُورَ قَالَتْ لِحَيَاةِ النُّفُوسِ يَا حَبِيبَتِي إِنَّ تَرْكَكِ وَامْتِنَاعِي عَنْكِ كُلُّهُ بِالرَّغْمِ عَنِّي
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malikata Budūra qālat li-Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi yā ḥabībatī inna tarkaki wa-imtināʿī ʿanki kulluhu bi-al-raghmi ʿannī
sentences.l: Then indeed the-Queen Budūr said to-Ḥayāt al-Nufūs: O my-beloved, indeed my-leaving-you and-my-holding-back from-you, all-of-it (is) with-the-reluctance from-me.
sentences.i: Then Queen Budūr said to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, “My dear, my leaving you alone and holding back from you has all been against my will.”
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, the narrator's way of turning to a new subject: Budūra is accusative after inna, with the diptote's -a. li-Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi, “to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs”: li- marks the one spoken to. Budūr now speaks to her as to a woman, with the feminine -ki. tark, “leaving”, and imtināʿ ʿan, Form VIII, “holding back from”, are verbal nouns. kulluhu bi-al-raghmi ʿannī, “all of it is against my will”: a sentence of its own standing as the predicate of inna. bi-al-raghmi ʿannī, the later language's way of saying “against my will”, for Classical raghman ʿannī: bi- here gives the manner.

sentences.t: وَحَكَتْ لَهَا عَلَى مَا جَرَى لَهَا مِنَ الِابْتِدَاءِ إِلَى الِانْتِهَاءِ وَأَرَتْ لَهَا نَفْسَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ḥakat lahā ʿalā mā jarā lahā mina al-ibtidāʾi ilā al-intihāʾi wa-arat lahā nafsahā
sentences.l: And-she-related to-her about what befell her from the-beginning to the-ending, and-showed to-her herself.
sentences.i: She told her all that had happened to her from beginning to end, and showed her what she was.
sentences.n: ḥakā li- … ʿalā, “to tell someone about”: li- marks the hearer, and ʿalā marks the matter told, a Middle Arabic use for Classical ḥakā lahu mā …. mina al-ibtidāʾi ilā al-intihāʾi, “from the beginning to the end”, a rhymed pair. arat lahā nafsahā, “she showed her herself”: arā, Form IV of raʾā, “to show”, takes two objects in Classical; here li- marks the one shown, as in the later language. She uncovers herself, so that the girl can see she is a woman. The hamza of الابتداء and الانتهاء is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهَا سَأَلْتُكِ بِاللّٰهِ إِلَّا مَا سَتَرْتِ عَلَيَّ وَأَخْفَيْتِ أَمْرِي حَتَّى يَجْمَعَنِي اللّٰهُ بِمَحْبُوبِي قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahā saʾaltuki bi-Allāhi illā mā satarti ʿalayya wa-akhfayti amrī ḥattā yajmaʿanī Allāhu bi-maḥbūbī Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-she-said to-her: I-ask-you by-God, (nothing) except that you-cover over-me and-hide my-affair, until brings-together-me God with-my-beloved Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: And she said to her, “I beg you by God to keep my secret and hide my case, until God brings me together with my beloved Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: saʾaltuki bi-Allāhi illā mā …, “I ask you by God, (I ask nothing) but that you …”, the set form of an earnest plea: bi- marks the one sworn by, and illā mā with the perfect gives what is asked. The shadda of الّا is printed, as is the hamza of سألتك and the shadda of عليّ. satara ʿalā, “to cover up for, keep someone's secret”. jamaʿa … bi-, “to bring together with”: bi- marks the one one is brought to. Qamari al-Zamāni stands in apposition to maḥbūbī, “my beloved”.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ يَكُونُ مَا يَكُونُ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika yakūnu mā yakūnu
sentences.l: And-after that, will-be what will-be.
sentences.i: After that, let come what may.”
sentences.n: yakūnu mā yakūnu, “what will be, will be”: the verb repeated in a relative clause leaves the outcome open.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print sets the name as two words, شهر زاد; they are kept as set.
